text:
Today, October 1, Virgin Islanders honor Contract Day.

After our ancestors took their freedom from chattel slavery in 1848, the Labor Act of 1849 created a new kind of bondage. Workers were bound to one plantation for a full year, with a day wage and restricted movement, able to change estates only on Contract Day. It was freedom in name only.

On October 1, 1878, when rumors of reform proved false, 30 years of frustration ignited the St. Croix Labor Rebellion, known to us as Fireburn. It was led by four women we revere as our Queens: Mary Thomas, Mathilda McBean, Susanna "Bottom Belly" Abrahamson, and Axeline "Queen Agnes" Salomon.

They demanded fair wages and the repeal of the Labor Act, and many paid with their lives. From their sacrifice came reforms that dismantled the labor system.

Today we honor our heritage and remember their courage. 🔥

This moment also calls for a hard look at the moral rot of a culture that made these students and administrators feel comfortable turning a blind eye to such a heinous, violent crime against this young woman. We have to do better.

text:
This is ILLEGAL.

Congress decides what gets funded, and the President is required to follow those decisions. That is NOT optional. 

And if you don’t believe me, take it from the Government Accountability Office, Congress’s non-partisan watchdog, who thinks it’s illegal too.

My Democrat and Republican colleagues and I on the House Appropriations Committee have spent the last year fighting over, negotiating, and deciding how every single dollar of this funding should be spent.

Trump & his Budget Director Russ Vought are now trying to get around all of that with something called a “pocket rescission.”

Here’s how it’s supposed to work: if the President wants to cancel funding Congress already approved, he sends Congress a request. Congress has 45 days to approve or reject that request. If Congress says no, the President has no choice but to release it. 

Except Trump waited until there were only FIVE DAYS left in the fiscal year.

He is denying Congress the opportunity to even make a decision, and it’s a clear violation of the Constitution.

The President does not get to just cancel $1 billion that Congress passed, and he himself signed into law without consulting Congress.

It’s time to close this loophole once and for all. 
https://t.co/v1ki1s8QkQ

RT @LongTimeHistory: U.S. citizen commits suicide after mom detained—blames ICE in his goodbye note.

"To the ICE agent who took away my mo…

reposted.text:
U.S. citizen commits suicide after mom detained—blames ICE in his goodbye note.

"To the ICE agent who took away my mom: I hope it was worth it," he wrote.

"I can’t handle any more injustice in this world."

His mom wasn't even person they were after—she didn't even match photo.

Minerva Terrones Dominguez had just gotten off a bus when agents said she "looked like someone" they had a warrant for.

A federal judge later ruled her detention unlawful.

But it was too late—her son was dead.

Samuel Gonzalez Terrones, 21, suffered from mental health issues—and relied on his mom as his main caregiver.

Incident occurred in San Bernardino, California—where the woman had lived for 33 years with no criminal record.

Posting first full length, English translated, and credited video here to help raise awareness.

My statement with @RepMcGovern and @RepGaramendi:  

We are deeply alarmed by increasing violence in Ethiopia, including the Ethiopian military strike last week on an aid convoy delivering assistance in Tigray.

The 2022 Pretoria Agreement that silenced the guns in Northern Ethiopia committed all parties to ceasing hostilities, protecting civilians, allowing humanitarian access to those affected, and undertaking comprehensive transitional justice to hold those responsible for human rights abuses and violations responsible. Unfortunately, this agreement has not been upheld, and these conditions have not been met.

This increased conflict threatens the entire country and the region as a whole, which is already reeling from the previous war in Northern Ethiopia and the devastating conflict in Sudan. Ordinary civilians are bearing the brunt of this violence.

text:
Veterans should be able to get support before they reach a crisis.

The Department of Veterans Affairs has announced two FY27 suicide prevention grants totaling $1.5 million to organizations serving South Texas Veterans and their families: $750,000 for the American GI Forum National Veterans Outreach Program and $750,000 for Chicanos Por La Causa.

The Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Suicide Prevention Grant Program supports community-based outreach, peer support, case management, benefits assistance, and connections to care, helping Veterans get support closer to home.

As a member of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies, I will continue working to make sure VA has the resources to reach Veterans in South Texas and connect them with the care and support they have earned.

If you or a Veteran you know needs immediate support, dial 988, then press 1 to reach the Veterans Crisis Line.

text:
South Texas students should not have to pay the price for cuts to federal education programs. More than $2 billion in Department of Education grants have already been discontinued or terminated across the country, and now the Administration is proposing even deeper cuts to education funding.

The Administration is now refusing to spend another $94.5 million in education funding already approved by Congress, including $24.9 million for programs that support students. On top of that, the Administration’s budget proposes cutting Department of Education funding by $12.3 billion. Their budget would eliminate 62 competitive and formula grant programs across K-12 education, special education, and higher education.

As a senior member of the Appropriations Committee, I have worked to secure federal education funding because I know what these investments mean for South Texas. Congress has the power of the purse, and funding approved by Congress should be used for the purposes Congress intended.

I will continue working to protect these investments and make sure our students, teachers, schools, and colleges have the resources they need.

New Jersey’s Nuclear Power Task Force is getting to work.

Nuclear already generates more than 40% of our electricity and 80% of our clean power. We’ve lifted a 50-year moratorium on new nuclear development and signed the Power NJ Act to pave the way for more nuclear power with strong protections for ratepayers.

And we’re doing it the right way – any new nuclear project must pass rigorous review by our Board of Public Utilities and Economic Development Authority and prove its benefits before breaking ground.

Now, experts from government, industry, and labor will help shape what comes next as we work to expand power generation, lower costs, and keep New Jersey competitive for the long term.

reposted.text:
Outsourcing AI regulation to a voluntary "pledge" conceived by Mark Zuckerberg and endorsed by tech CEOs over a private White House lunch is a recipe for disaster.  

"Self-regulation" by tech giants is a proven failure. The last time Meta promised to police itself, turned out it was hiding evidence that its platforms actively harm kids. Repeating this mistake with AI leaves the public dangerously exposed. 

AI companies are already bound by existing laws, but the White House has generally stopped enforcing laws against the wealthy and powerful. State AGs should step up, halt lawbreaking, and promote real deterrence, including through holding individual executives accountable.  

Congress also needs to legislate. We have a long history of regulating risky, transformative industries like banking, pharmaceuticals, and nuclear power. These tools include mandatory testing, truly independent supervision, and break-ups that end conflicts of interest.  

Ultimately, reckoning with AI will also require reckoning with our broader crisis of governance. All three branches have become severely deformed. Against this backdrop it might be tempting to outsource regulation to these private actors, but it would be a serious mistake. 

Our public institutions must decide the trajectory of these powerful technologies, not the firms whose breakneck pace and financial conflicts brought us here. 

My piece in @nytopinion: https://t.co/j0Nrp2JWqi

https://t.co/GpT22K4Qwl

text:
Last year, Donald Trump and Congressional Republicans rammed through their Big Ugly Bill which decimated healthcare and nutrition assistance for American families to pay for tax breaks for billionaires.

Starting today, New York State and local governments will be forced to pay $220 million a year to make up for these cuts to SNAP, the nutritional assistance program. That means less money for education, public safety, infrastructure, and environmental protection.

The real cost falls on the millions of Americans who rely on SNAP to put food on the table. Since the bill passed, 5 million people nationwide have already lost access, including 1 million children. Most of those who still depend on it are seniors, children, and people with disabilities. When I say a budget is a reflection of our values, this is exactly what I mean - and Donald Trump is showing our communities that he does not care about the real needs of the American people.

https://t.co/iLwSfBpwm0

Today and always, our hearts are with the victims, survivors, and the entire Las Vegas community as we work to prevent such senseless acts of gun violence.
